label: Bardaisan of Edessa (Bar-Daisan)
description: Bardaisan of Edessa (Bar-Daiṣan, c. 154 — c. 222 CE), Syriac Christian philosopher and court-figure at the Abgarid court of Osrhoene (Edessa). Known almost exclusively through the dialogue Book of the Laws of the Countries (Syriac: Ktābā d-nāmōsē d-aṯrawātā), composed by his disciple Philippus, which presents Bardaisan in conversation with his pupils on fate, free will, and divine providence. Trained in Greek philosophy and Syriac learning, Bardaisan articulated what modern scholars characterize as a tripartite causal scheme: nature governs the bodily/physical sphere; fate (heimarmenē) operates via planetary influences in the sphere of contingent circumstances (birth, health, wealth, untimely death); but freedom (ḥērūtā / autexousion) is reserved for the sphere of moral action. He thus partially conceded astrological causation while preserving moral responsibility — a position later adopted and reworked by Eusebius (PE VI.10), Diodore of Tarsus, and Gregory of Nyssa (Contra Fatum). His signature argument is the nomima barbarika ('barbarian customs'): if the planetary configurations were causally sufficient for human behavior, all peoples born under the same constellations would behave identically; in fact, lawcodes diverge sharply by ethnos (Brahmans, Persians, Geli, Bactrians, Britons, Parthians), demonstrating that custom and choice override stellar influence. The argument circulates through Eusebius and becomes a standard topos in Patristic anti-astrological polemic. Bardaisan was condemned by later Syriac orthodoxy (Ephrem the Syrian, Madrāšē against Heresies) for cosmogonic dualism and views on the resurrection body, though the extent to which the Book of the Laws faithfully represents him remains contested (Drijvers 1966; Possekel 1999). Critical edition + English translation: H.J.W. Drijvers, The Book of the Laws of Countries (Assen 1965; reprinted Gorgias 2007).

works: Book of the Laws of the Countries (via Philippus)
Lost: hymns, cosmological treatises, Against Marcion

label: Gregory of Nyssa
description: Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335 — c. 395 CE), Cappadocian bishop, younger brother of Basil of Caesarea and friend of Gregory of Nazianzus. Author of the most philosophically sophisticated theological anthropology of the fourth century. His De Hominis Opificio (PG 44, 124B–256C; SC 6, Laplace–Daniélou 1944; new edition forthcoming GNO) — written c. 379 CE to complete Basil's Hexaemeron — argues in chapters 16 and 24 that the imago Dei (κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ) consists essentially in human reason endowed with αὐτεξούσιον (self-determination): God's freedom from external compulsion is the ontological model for which human moral freedom is the created copy. To compel virtue would be self-contradictory, since virtue presupposes a free agent. In De Anima et Resurrectione (PG 46, 11–160; the Macrinia-dialogue, c. 380 CE; SC 614, Maraval 2022) and the Catechetical Oration (Oratio Catechetica Magna, esp. cc. 5–8 on the fall and 16–24 on incarnation; PG 45, 9–105; GCS Srawley 1903; SC 453, Winling 2000), he develops the synergism of grace and freedom: salvation is effected by divine action which presupposes and elicits, but does not coerce, human cooperation. Contra Eunomium (GNO I–II, Jaeger 1921–60; SC forthcoming) defends divine simplicity and infinity against Eunomian rationalism, with consequences for the theology of providence. Contra Fatum (GNO III.2, McDonough 1987) deploys Bardaisanian nomima barbarika arguments against Manichaean and astrological determinism in dialogue with a pagan philosopher. Gregory's anthropology bridges Origen's Platonism and the later Greek tradition (Maximus the Confessor, John Damascene); his account of human freedom as ontological participation in divine freedom is a key resource for Eastern theological accounts of autexousion that resist Augustinian gratia irresistibilis.

works: Oratio Catechetica Magna (PG 45; GCS Srawley; SC 453)

label: Maximus the Confessor
description: Maximus the Confessor (c. 580 — 13 August 662 CE), Byzantine monk, theologian, and martyr, born in Constantinople (Vita 1) or Palestine (Syriac Life). After a court career under Heraclius (c. 610–614), he entered the monastery at Chrysopolis, then Cyzicus, and after the Persian invasion (626) emigrated to North Africa. He became the principal Greek theological opponent of Monothelitism — the imperial doctrine that Christ had only one (divine) will. In the Disputatio cum Pyrrho (645 CE, Carthage; PG 91, 287–354; new critical edition Doucet, SC 478 (forthcoming) / Riou 1973 thesis), Maximus debates the deposed Patriarch Pyrrhus and articulates the distinction between φυσικὸν θέλημα (natural will — the constitutive volitional faculty inhering in human nature, oriented teleologically to the good) and γνωμικὸν θέλημα (gnomic will — the deliberative, opinion-forming inclination of the fallen rational creature, characterized by ignorance, hesitation, and the possibility of vice). He attributes only the former to Christ, since the gnomic will is a post-lapsarian mode of willing arising from finitude and ignorance, incompatible with the hypostatic union. The Ambigua ad Iohannem (PG 91, 1031–1417; edited Constas, DOML 28–29, 2014) and Ambigua ad Thomam, alongside the Opuscula theologica et polemica (PG 91, 9–286; Sherwood, Berthold), develop the further distinction between τὸ θέλειν (the natural willing-power) and τὸ πῶς θέλειν (the manner of willing — properly the locus of moral choice). Condemned at the imperial council of 662, his tongue and right hand were cut off; he died in exile in Lazica. Posthumously rehabilitated at Constantinople III (680–681 CE), which adopted his dyothelite Christology as Catholic doctrine. His distinction structures the later Eastern account of free will and remains the principal Greek answer to the question of whether divine and human freedom are univocal: they share πῶς θέλειν only analogically.

scholarly_refs: Tollefsen 2008 (The Christocentric Cosmology of St Maximus)

label: Book of the Laws of the Countries (Ktābā d-nāmōsē d-aṯrawātā)
description: Syriac dialogue composed by Philippus, a disciple of Bardaisan, preserving (with what scholars characterize as substantial editorial framing) the teaching of Bardaisan of Edessa on fate, providence, and free will. Composed in Edessa, likely between c. 196 and c. 230 CE. The frame: Bardaisan converses with disciples (Avida, Bar-Yamma, Šemšegram, Philippus) over an extended philosophical discussion. The dialogue advances a tripartite causal scheme — nature (kyānā), fate (heimarmenē / helqā, planetary influence over bodily/economic contingencies), and freedom (ḥērūtā, the moral sphere) — and culminates in the celebrated nomima barbarika argument: divergent lawcodes among Brahmans (vegetarianism, sexual abstinence), Persians (consanguineous marriage), Geli, Bactrians, Britons, Parthians, Amazons, Romans, and the converted (Christians) demonstrate that planetary positions cannot determine human moral conduct. The argument circulates via Greek translation in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica VI.10 (and via Pseudo-Clement, Recognitiones IX), becoming a standard Patristic anti-astrological topos taken up by Gregory of Nyssa, Diodore of Tarsus, and others. Critical edition + English translation: H.J.W. Drijvers, The Book of the Laws of Countries: Dialogue on Fate of Bardaiṣan of Edessa, Semitic Texts with Translations 3 (Assen: van Gorcum, 1965; reprinted Gorgias Press, 2007). Earlier edition: W. Cureton, Spicilegium Syriacum (London 1855).

label: Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus (Λόγος προτρεπτικὸς πρὸς Ἕλληνας)
description: Clement of Alexandria's Protrepticus ('Exhortation to the Greeks', c. 195 CE), the first of his three-part programmatic trilogy (Protrepticus → Paedagogus → Stromateis), summons pagan readers from polytheism, mystery cults, and philosophical error to the Logos. Twelve chapters in the standard division; structured around the contrast between the Greek myths and rites (chs. 1–4) and the true Logos who calls humanity to its dignity as εἰκὼν θεοῦ (image of God). The work assumes and presupposes free human capacity to respond to divine address: the very form of the protrepsis (exhortation) is incompatible with determinism. Critical editions: O. Stählin (GCS 12, 1905; rev. Treu 1972); C. Mondésert, SC 2 (Cerf, 1949; rev. ed. 2004 with introduction by A. Plassart); A. Heuser-Hofmann (Fontes Christiani 60). English: G.W. Butterworth (LCL 92, 1919). French: M. Caster, A. Plassart (SC 2).

label: Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus (Παιδαγωγός)
description: Clement of Alexandria's Paedagogus ('The Tutor', c. 197–203 CE), the second of his trilogy. Three books: I treats the Logos as παιδαγωγός (moral tutor) of Christian souls; II–III provide concrete moral instruction on food, drink, dress, sexual conduct, baths, sleep. The pedagogical framework presupposes that the soul is capable of moral formation through free response to divine instruction — a position incompatible with Valentinian and Marcionite predeterminism. Critical editions: O. Stählin (GCS 12, 1905; rev. Treu/Früchtel/Treu 1972); H.-I. Marrou, M. Harl, C. Mondésert, C. Matray, SC 70 (Cerf 1960), SC 108 (Cerf 1965), SC 158 (Cerf 1970). English: S. Wood, FOTC 23 (1954).

label: Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis (Στρωματεῖς)
description: Clement of Alexandria's Stromateis ('Miscellanies', c. 198–215 CE) in eight books, the third and largest work of his trilogy, intended for the more advanced 'gnostic' Christian reader. Of greatest relevance to debates on free will and moral responsibility are: Book II (esp. II.6–15) on faith, choice (προαίρεσις), assent (συγκατάθεσις), and the will, where Clement reworks the Stoic theory of assent (echoing Chrysippus, Epictetus) to defend Christian αὐτεξούσιον (self-determination) against both Valentinian psychic determinism and Marcionite Demiurge-blame; Book IV.23–24 on the perfect gnostic and the relation of grace and freedom; Book VII on Christian piety and the gnostic's apatheia; and Book VIII (the so-called 'logical' book, a notebook of philosophical materials) on demonstration, causation, and assent. Clement's signature move is the synergism of grace and human cooperation: God draws, but does not compel; faith is itself a free act, but one that arises only because the Logos has elicited it. Critical editions: O. Stählin (GCS 15, 1906 for Books I–VI; GCS 17, 1909 for Books VII–VIII; rev. Früchtel/Treu); A. Le Boulluec (SC 38, 278, 279, 428, 446, 463; Cerf, 1981–2001); P. Descourtieux (SC 446 Book VI, 1999). English: J. Ferguson, FOTC 85 (1991) for Books I–III.

label: Augustine, De Libero Arbitrio (On the Free Choice of the Will)
description: Augustine of Hippo, De Libero Arbitrio Voluntatis ('On Free Choice of the Will'), three books, the first major Latin Christian philosophical treatise dedicated specifically to the free will problem. Book I begun c. 388 CE at Rome (or shortly after his return to Africa in 388); Books II–III completed c. 391–395 CE at Hippo (cf. Retractationes I.9). A dialogue between Augustinus and Evodius. The anti-Manichean argument-structure: God is the source of all good; evil is real but is not a substance — it is the disordered direction of a created will away from immutable to mutable goods; evil therefore originates not in matter or in a second principle, but in the free choice (liberum arbitrium voluntatis) of a created rational being. Book I treats moral evil and the inner experience of choice; Book II argues from the existence of free will to its goodness (since rational creatures must have voluntary motion); Book III addresses divine foreknowledge, the origin of the soul, and the rectitude of God's permission of evil. The later anti-Pelagian Augustine of c. 412+ would carefully retract elements he saw as exploitable by Pelagius (cf. Retr. I.9, De Praedestinatione Sanctorum), but never disavowed the core argument. Critical editions: W.M. Green, CCSL 29 (Brepols 1970); CSEL 74 (Migne PL 32, 1221–1310 baseline); F.-J. Thonnard, Bibliothèque Augustinienne 6 (Desclée 1941; rev. 1976). English: T. Williams (Hackett 1993); P. King (Cambridge 2010). French: BA 6.

metadata.author: Augustine of Hippo
metadata.date_composed: Book I c. 388; Books II–III c. 391 — 395 CE

label: Augustine, Confessiones VIII (Two Wills)
description: Augustine of Hippo, Confessiones Book VIII (composed c. 397–401 CE) — the locus classicus of the duae voluntates ('two wills') doctrine that would reshape Western philosophical psychology. Conf. VIII.5.10 — 8.19: Augustine narrates the inner conflict that preceded his conversion at Milan (386 CE), formulating the phenomenology of internally divided willing: 'velle meum tenebat inimicus, et inde mihi catenam fecerat et constrinxerat me… ita duae voluntates meae, una vetus, alia nova, illa carnalis, illa spiritalis, confligebant inter se atque discordando dissipabant animam meam' (Conf. VIII.5.10). The argument that 'the mind commands the body and is at once obeyed; the mind commands itself and is resisted' (VIII.9.21) replaces a faculty-psychology of separate appetites with a single self-divided will whose internal struggle is constitutive of fallen freedom. Critical editions: L. Verheijen, CCSL 27 (Brepols 1981); M. Skutella, BSGRT (Teubner 1934; rev. Jürgens 1969, Solignac BA 13–14). English: H. Chadwick (OUP 1991); M. Boulding (NCP I/1, 1997). French: P. de Labriolle (Belles Lettres, Budé); BA 13–14.

label: John Chrysostom, Homiliae in Epistulam ad Romanos (Homilies on Romans)
description: John Chrysostom's series of 32 homilies on Paul's Epistle to the Romans (PG 60, 391–682), delivered at Antioch between c. 391 and c. 397 CE while Chrysostom was still presbyter under bishop Flavian. The series is the longest and most carefully ordered of his Pauline expositions. Homily 16 (on Romans 9:1–18), Homily 17 (on Romans 9:19–33), and Homily 18 (on Romans 10) contain his sustained reading of Rom 9:14–24 (the Pharaoh-and-vessels passage), which he interprets — against any deterministic predestinarian construal — as an a fortiori argument: if the potter has authority over the clay, much more does God justly permit reprobation in foreknowledge of obstinate refusal. He preserves a robust autexousion and identifies fault (αἰτία) as resting in Pharaoh's hardened heart, not in divine arbitrary decree. The Homilies on Romans were profoundly influential on Theodore of Mopsuestia and on the Antiochene exegetical tradition, and were read in the East as a charter for synergism against Western Augustinian readings of Rom 9. Critical text: F. Field, Joannis Chrysostomi Interpretatio Omnium Epistolarum Paulinarum, vol. I (Oxford 1849), reprinted in PG 60. NPNF series 1, vol. 11 (English). New SC edition partial (Voicu et al., in progress).

metadata.author: John Chrysostom
editions: Voicu et al., SC in progress

label: Maximus the Confessor, Ambigua ad Iohannem
description: Maximus the Confessor's Ambigua ad Iohannem ('Difficulties for John', composed c. 628 — 630 CE while Maximus was in North Africa), 71 sections (counting Ambigua 6–71 in the traditional numbering; preceded by Ambigua ad Thomam, 5 sections). Addressed to John, bishop of Cyzicus, the work resolves passages of Gregory of Nazianzus that had been deployed by Origenist readers. Maximus develops the doctrine of the λόγοι τῶν ὄντων (logoi of beings) — the divine intentions according to which each created being exists — as the alternative to Origenist pre-existence of souls; the relation of natural movement (κίνησις) to created freedom; and the structure of human willing in relation to Christ's hypostatic union. Ambiguum 7 (on Gregory of Nazianzus, Or. 14.7) is the locus classicus for Maximus's distinction between motion toward God as natural fulfillment and motion away from God as gnomic deviation. Critical edition: Nicholas Constas, On Difficulties in the Church Fathers: The Ambigua, Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library 28–29 (Harvard 2014, Greek + English). Predecessor edition: PG 91, 1031–1417. French: J.-Cl. Larchet, E. Ponsoye (Suresnes 1994).

label: Maximus the Confessor, Opuscula theologica et polemica
description: Maximus the Confessor's Opuscula theologica et polemica (PG 91, 9–286), a collection of 27 short dogmatic and polemical pieces composed between c. 633 and c. 650 CE addressing the monothelite and monenergist controversies. Several are foundational for the dyothelite distinction between natural will and gnomic will, e.g. Opusculum 1 (to Marinus, on the two energies), Opusculum 3, Opusculum 16 (on the Tomos to Marinus). They predate and prepare the Disputatio cum Pyrrho (645). Critical text: PG 91; partial new editions in CCSG. English: A. Louth, Maximus the Confessor (Routledge 1996, selections); B. Daley, ed., Maximus Confessor: Selected Writings (Paulist 1985). French: Cl. Larchet, E. Ponsoye, Opuscules théologiques et polémiques (Cerf 1998).

label: Gregory of Nyssa, De Anima et Resurrectione (Macrinia)
description: Gregory of Nyssa, De Anima et Resurrectione (Περὶ ψυχῆς καὶ ἀναστάσεως, c. 380 CE), a Platonic dialogue in form — the so-called Macrinia — staged between Gregory and his dying sister Macrina shortly after the death of Basil (379 CE). Treats the soul's nature, immortality, the passions, eschatology, and the relation between free human choice and the universal apokatastasis envisaged at the end. Argues that the soul retains αὐτεξούσιον (self-determination) as a constitutive feature of its rational nature, even in its purification post mortem. Critical edition: A. Spira, GNO III.3 (Brill 2014; new editio maior); previously PG 46, 11–160. SC 614, ed. P. Maraval (Cerf 2022). English: V.W. Callahan, FOTC 58 (CUA Press 1967); C.P. Roth (St Vladimir's 1993). French: Maraval, SC 614 (2022); J. Terrieux (Cerf 1995).

label: Gregory of Nyssa, Oratio Catechetica Magna
description: Gregory of Nyssa, Oratio Catechetica Magna (Λόγος κατηχητικὸς ὁ μέγας, c. 385 CE), in 40 chapters, a comprehensive catechetical exposition of Christian doctrine for catechists addressing Greeks, Jews, and Christians. Chapters 5–8 treat the fall and the origin of evil — articulating that evil is privatio boni (the absence of good) arising from the misuse of the human capacity for autonomous choice, not from divine causation or material substance. Chapters 16–24 develop the incarnation as the divine economy of restoration that respects rather than overrides created freedom. Critical edition: J.H. Srawley, GCS (CUP 1903; rev. ed. with new readings forthcoming GNO); E. Mühlenberg, GNO III.4 (Brill 1996). SC 453, ed. R. Winling (Cerf 2000). English: J.H. Srawley (London 1917, rev.); NPNF 2.5.

label: Gregory of Nyssa, Contra Eunomium
description: Gregory of Nyssa, Contra Eunomium (Πρὸς Εὐνόμιον ἀντιρρητικός, c. 380 — 383 CE) in three books (with multiple sub-divisions), the central anti-Eunomian work of the Cappadocian response to the radical Anomoian theology of Eunomius of Cyzicus. Defends divine infinity, simplicity, and the impossibility of human discursive grasp of the divine essence, against Eunomius's claim to scientific knowledge of God through the name 'unbegotten' (ἀγέννητος). Indirectly grounds Gregory's anthropology of freedom: since the divine infinite essence is unknowable, the human approach to God is by progressive participation (epektasis), which requires an enduring αὐτεξούσιον. Critical edition: W. Jaeger, GNO I (Books I and II; 1921, rev. 1960), GNO II (Book III; 1925, rev. 1960; Brill 1990 reprint). English: S.G. Hall (in NPNF 2.5; new translation in Maraval-Winling forthcoming). French: B. Pottier, Dieu et le Christ selon Grégoire de Nysse (1994, partial); SC forthcoming.

label: Tertullian, De Praescriptione Haereticorum
description: Tertullian, De Praescriptione Haereticorum ('The Prescription against Heretics', c. 200 CE), a juridical-rhetorical treatise applying Roman legal language of praescriptio (a procedural bar) to debarrring heretics from appeal to Scripture. The argument is foundational for the orthodox doctrine of the regula fidei and the apostolic transmission of doctrine, but bears on free will indirectly: Tertullian's juridical anthropology presupposes that the human will is genuinely accountable before divine judgement, and that the public determinability of orthodox belief presupposes free human consent to apostolic teaching. Critical edition: R.F. Refoulé, CCSL 1 (Brepols 1954); P. de Labriolle, SC 46 (Cerf 1957). English: S. Thelwall, ANF 3; G.D. Dunn (Routledge 2004).

label: Tertullian, De Resurrectione Carnis
description: Tertullian, De Resurrectione Carnis ('On the Resurrection of the Flesh', c. 210 — 213 CE) in 63 chapters, addressed against Marcionite and Gnostic dualism that denied bodily resurrection. The argument grounds Christian eschatology in the bodily integrity of the human being and in the moral accountability of the embodied person before divine judgement. Bears on free will via its juridical framing: the resurrection is intelligible only if the embodied agent is the morally responsible subject of judgement. Critical edition: J.G.Ph. Borleffs, CCSL 2 (Brepols 1954); E. Evans, Tertullian's Treatise on the Resurrection (London: SPCK 1960, with English). ANF 3 (Eng., Holmes). Possibly the most carefully argued of Tertullian's anti-Marcionite treatises.

label: Pseudo-Clement (Anonymous)
description: Anonymous Christian author(s) of the corpus of writings transmitted under the name of Clement of Rome but in fact composed in Greek-speaking Syria, probably in the early-mid third century CE (c. 220 — 260, with some materials possibly earlier). The corpus comprises the so-called Pseudo-Clementine Homiliae (20 homilies, preserved entire in Greek) and Recognitiones (10 books, preserved in the Latin translation of Rufinus of Aquileia, c. 406 CE; also partially in Syriac). Both works share a common substratum, the so-called Grundschrift (Quellenschrift), now lost. The corpus depicts a series of disputations between Peter and Simon Magus, framed within a romance of Clement's recognition of his lost family. Important for free will: Recognitiones Book III contains an extended disputation on free will against the deterministic 'genesis' (γένεσις, planetary destiny) of Simon Magus; Book IX (esp. Recogn. IX.19–29) and Homilies 14.3–11 deploy the Bardaisanian nomima barbarika argument against astrological fatalism, depending on Bardaisan via the Book of the Laws of the Countries. Critical editions: B. Rehm, GCS 42 (Homiliae, 1953; rev. Strecker 1969, 1992); B. Rehm — F. Paschke, GCS 51 (Recognitiones, 1965; rev. Strecker 1994). English: T. Smith, ANF 8; new SC edition forthcoming.

label: Pseudo-Clement, Recognitiones (Latin translation by Rufinus of Aquileia)
description: Pseudo-Clementine Recognitiones, ten books, transmitted in the Latin translation of Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 406 CE). Original Greek lost (apart from quotations and Syriac fragments). Composed c. 220 — 260 CE in Greek-speaking Syria. Cast as a romance: Clement of Rome's recognition of his long-lost family, intercalated with extended theological-philosophical disputations between Peter and his opponents (Simon Magus chief among them). For the free-will debate, Recogn. III (the Caesarea disputations) contains Peter's anti-Simonian arguments grounding moral responsibility in human autexousion against Simon's astrological determinism; Recogn. VIII–X (the Tripolis–Laodicea–Antioch disputations) contains the elaborate anti-astrological apologetic — especially Recogn. IX.19–29 — in which a 'Christian philosopher' (Niceta, Aquila, or a barbarian sage) deploys the Bardaisanian nomima barbarika argument against the genesis (planetary destiny) of Simon. The disputation is drawn from Bardaisan's Book of the Laws of the Countries, via the lost common source (Grundschrift) shared with the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, and constitutes the most extensive Patristic redeployment of Bardaisan's argument outside Eusebius (PE VI.10). Critical edition: B. Rehm — F. Paschke, GCS 51 (1965; rev. Strecker 1994). English: T. Smith, ANF 8 (1886). French: A. Schneider, A. Le Boulluec, et al., SC forthcoming.

metadata.author: Pseudo-Clement (anonymous)
metadata.original_language: Greek (lost); preserved in Latin (Rufinus) and Syriac

label: Pseudo-Clement, Homiliae
description: Pseudo-Clementine Homiliae, 20 homilies, preserved entire in Greek, composed c. 220 — 260 CE in Greek-speaking Syria, sharing with the Recognitiones a common lost Grundschrift. The homilies frame Clement of Rome as the narrator of theological disputations between Peter and Simon Magus, with substantial 'Jewish-Christian' theological positions (rejection of much of the Hebrew Bible's anthropomorphic accounts of God under the rubric of 'false pericopes', strict monotheism, baptismal soteriology). Hom. XIV.3–11 contains the parallel anti-astrological argument (nomima barbarika) preserved more fully in Recogn. IX, drawn from Bardaisan. Critical edition: B. Rehm, Die Pseudoklementinen I: Homilien, GCS 42 (Berlin 1953; rev. Strecker 1969, 1992). English: T. Smith, ANF 8 (1886). New SC edition forthcoming.

label: Maximus the Confessor: Natural Will vs. Gnomic Will (Disp. Pyrrh.; Opusc. 1, 3)
description: Maximus the Confessor's distinction between the natural will (φυσικὸν θέλημα) and the gnomic will (γνωμικὸν θέλημα), articulated at the Disputatio cum Pyrrho (645 CE, PG 91, 287–354) and in Opuscula theologica et polemica 1, 3, 16 (PG 91, 9–286). Structure of argument — (Premise 1) Will is a property of nature, not of hypostasis: every nature has its own willing-power as a constitutive feature, so that two natures imply two wills, not one. (Premise 2) Christ has two natures (divine and human, Chalcedon, 451), each preserving its own properties intact and unconfused. (Conclusion 1) Therefore Christ has two natural wills — one divine and one human, in perfect harmony. (Premise 3) The gnomic will (γνώμη) is not the natural willing-power but rather a deliberative mode of willing arising from ignorance, hesitation, and the possibility of error; it is a property of fallen, finite, post-lapsarian rational agents, not of nature as such. (Conclusion 2) Christ, being divine in his hypostasis and lacking ignorance and corruption, has no gnomic will; his human will, hypostatically united to the divine Logos, wills naturally and unhesitatingly in accord with the divine will, without the dialectical agon characteristic of fallen human deliberation. This distinction is the principal Greek answer to the question whether divine and human freedom are univocal: they share τὸ θέλειν (the willing-power) by nature, but only analogically share τὸ πῶς θέλειν (the manner of willing). The argument is decisive against monothelitism (the imperial doctrine that Christ had only one will, of the Heraclian and Constans-II era), and is adopted at the Sixth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople III, 680–681).

metadata.author: Maximus the Confessor
premises: P1: Will is a property of nature, not of hypostasis (per Chalcedon).
P2: Christ has two natures, each with its own intact properties.
P3: Gnomic willing (γνώμη) is a deliberative mode arising from ignorance and finitude, proper to fallen creatures, not to nature as such.
metadata.conclusion: Christ has two natural wills (one divine, one human, in harmony) and no gnomic will. Divine and human freedom share τὸ θέλειν by nature but only analogically share τὸ πῶς θέλειν.

label: Bardaisan: Nomima Barbarika (Book of the Laws of the Countries)
description: Bardaisan of Edessa's argument from divergent ethnic lawcodes (νόμιμα βαρβαρικά / 'barbarian customs') against astrological determinism, preserved in the Book of the Laws of the Countries (early 3rd c. CE) and quoted at length in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica VI.10. Structure — (Premise 1) If planetary configurations at birth (γένεσις, helqā) were causally sufficient to determine human moral conduct, then all persons born under the same constellation should behave identically. (Premise 2) The configuration of stars is uniform across the inhabited world; the same constellation appears at the same hour wherever children are born within its sweep. (Premise 3) Empirical observation: the customs of nations sharply diverge by ethnos rather than by astrological hour — Brahmans practice vegetarianism and sexual abstinence; Persians and Magi marry close kin (mothers, sisters, daughters); the Geli of the Caspian abstain from luxury garments; Bactrians and Britons hold property and women in common; among the converted (Christians), regardless of ethnos and natal star, common moral norms prevail (rejection of murder, theft, fornication). (Conclusion) The divergence is explicable only on the supposition that human moral conduct is not determined by stellar configuration but by νόμος (custom/law) and the ḥērūtā (freedom) of moral choice. The argument concedes a limited astral causality over external contingencies (health, wealth, illness, untimely death) — the sphere of fate proper — while reserving the moral sphere to free human agency. The argument circulates in Greek translation via Eusebius (PE VI.10) and via Pseudo-Clement (Recogn. IX.19–29, Hom. XIV), becoming the standard Patristic anti-astrological topos taken up by Gregory of Nyssa (Contra Fatum, GNO III.2), Diodore of Tarsus, Origen (Philocalia 23), and many others.

label: Gregory of Nyssa: Image-of-God Argument for Autexousion (De Hom. Opif. 16; Cat. Or.)
description: Gregory of Nyssa's foundational anthropological argument that human αὐτεξούσιον (self-determination) is the constitutive feature of the imago Dei, articulated in De Hominis Opificio chapters 16 and 24 (PG 44, 177D — 184C; 224B — 229A; SC 6) and reaffirmed in Oratio Catechetica Magna chapters 5 and 21 (GCS Srawley; SC 453). Structure — (Premise 1) The biblical claim that humanity was created κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ (Gen 1:26) requires identifying what feature of divine being is reflected in the human creature. (Premise 2) God's essential mode of being includes absolute freedom from external compulsion: God acts always according to his nature without coercion. (Premise 3) For the human creature to be a genuine εἰκών of this divine reality, the human must possess a created participation in self-determining agency — αὐτεξούσιον. (Premise 4) Compelled virtue is a self-contradiction: virtue requires a free agent, since a forced act has no moral worth. (Conclusion) The imago Dei consists essentially in human autexousion. From this it follows that (a) divine providence operates synergistically, eliciting but not coercing human cooperation; (b) salvation cannot be effected by divine fiat against human free response, which would be self-defeating; (c) the post-lapsarian retention of autexousion (in attenuated form) grounds both ongoing moral responsibility and the possibility of restoration. The position structures Gregory's account in De Anima et Resurrectione of the soul's path through purgation toward apokatastasis: even in its purification post mortem the soul retains the constitutive freedom that makes it the image of God.

metadata.author: Gregory of Nyssa
loci_classici: De Anima et Resurrectione (PG 46, 11–160; SC 614, on post-mortem retention)
premises: P1: The imago Dei (Gen 1:26) requires identifying a feature of divine being reflected in humanity.
P2: God's essential mode is freedom from external compulsion.
P3: A genuine image of this freedom requires created participation in self-determination (autexousion).
P4: Compelled virtue is self-contradictory; virtue presupposes free agency.
metadata.conclusion: The imago Dei consists essentially in autexousion. Divine providence is synergistic, not coercive; salvation respects rather than overrides created freedom.

label: Clement of Alexandria: Grace–Freedom Synergy via Stoic Assent (Strom. II.6–15)
description: Clement of Alexandria's argument in Stromateis II.6–15 (and re-affirmed in Strom. IV.23–24) that Christian salvation involves the cooperation (συνέργεια) of divine grace and human αὐτεξούσιον, mediated by the Stoic theory of προαίρεσις (rational choice) and συγκατάθεσις (assent). Structure — (Premise 1) The Stoic theory of assent (Chrysippus, via Cicero De Fato; Epictetus, Disc. I.1, II.6): external impressions (φαντασίαι) do not compel action; the rational soul retains the power to assent or withhold assent, and this assent is the agent's own, not a function of external causes. (Premise 2) Faith (πίστις) is itself an act of free assent to the divine λόγος: 'faith is the consent of the soul' (Strom. II.2.8). (Premise 3) But human nature is wounded, and assent to the good is not effortlessly achieved; the Logos must draw the soul (Protr. ad fin.; Strom. VII), thereby grounding the necessity of grace. (Premise 4) Yet drawing is not compelling: the grammar of προτροπή (exhortation) and διδαχή (teaching) is incompatible with coercion. (Conclusion) Christian salvation is a genuine synergy: God's grace elicits, but does not compel, the assent of the soul; the soul's assent is genuinely its own (αὐτεξούσιον), but is itself a gift of the Logos who has elicited it. This position — what Karamanolis 2021 calls a 'soft synergism' — sets Clement apart from later Augustinian monergism and from radical Valentinian psychic determinism. Clement's signature theological innovation, as identified by Jourdan and Karamanolis, is the conceptualization of Providence as an 'acting final cause' — fusing Stoic efficient causality with Platonic divine transcendence — which permits him to reject astrological heimarmenē (Strom. I.17.81–87, VI.17.157–162) while preserving universal rational order.

label: Augustine: Anti-Manichean Argument in De Libero Arbitrio (Books I–III)
description: Augustine of Hippo's foundational anti-Manichean argument in De Libero Arbitrio (Books I–III, c. 388 — 395 CE; ed. Green CCSL 29, Thonnard BA 6) that moral evil originates not in matter or in a co-eternal evil principle, but in the free choice (liberum arbitrium voluntatis) of created rational beings. Structure — (Premise 1) God, the source of all being, is essentially good; whatever has being from God has being-as-good (cf. De Lib. Arb. I.1.1; Plotinian-Neoplatonic ontology of good as convertible with being). (Premise 2) Evil is real but is not a substance; it is the privatio boni — the disordered direction of a created will away from the immutable good toward mutable goods (De Lib. Arb. II.19.53 — 20.54; III.1.1 — 5.13). (Premise 3) The free choice of will (liberum arbitrium voluntatis) is itself a good — a created good — without which rational creatures could not achieve genuine moral worth (De Lib. Arb. II.1.3; II.18.49 — 19.53). (Premise 4) Free choice is therefore necessary to creaturely flourishing, even though it is the metaphysical condition for the possibility of moral evil. (Premise 5) God's foreknowledge does not necessitate human action: foreknowing that an act will be done voluntarily is not foreknowing-it-as-necessitated (De Lib. Arb. III.2.4 — 4.11; the argument anticipated and refined later in De Civitate Dei V.9–10). (Conclusion) Moral evil originates in the free choice of created wills, not in a Manichean co-eternal evil principle or in matter. The created good of free will is preserved as the metaphysical foundation of moral responsibility, while accountability for evil is located firmly in the created agent. — Important caveat: the later Augustine of the anti-Pelagian period (412+) carefully retracts what he saw as exploitable formulations of this work for Pelagian self-sufficiency (cf. Retractationes I.9), insisting that post-lapsarian liberum arbitrium retains the bare metaphysical capacity but requires gratia operans and gratia cooperans for any saving good. The De Lib. Arb. is not disavowed but reinterpreted in the light of De Spiritu et Littera (412), De Natura et Gratia (415), and the predestinarian late works.

metadata.author: Augustine of Hippo
premises: P1: God is the source of all being and is essentially good.
P2: Evil is privatio boni, the disordered direction of will from immutable to mutable goods.
P3: Free choice (liberum arbitrium voluntatis) is itself a created good.
P4: Free choice is necessary to creaturely flourishing.
P5: God's foreknowledge does not necessitate voluntary action.
metadata.conclusion: Moral evil originates in created free choice, not in a co-eternal evil principle. Free will is preserved as a created good and as the foundation of moral responsibility.
metadata.later_revision: Anti-Pelagian Augustine (412+) preserves but restricts: post-lapsarian liberum arbitrium retains the bare metaphysical capacity but is impotent toward saving good without gratia operans / gratia cooperans (cf. De Gratia et Lib. Arb. 426–427).
scholarly_refs: Wetzel 1992 (Augustine and the Limits of Virtue)

label: Valentinus
description: Valentinus (fl. c. 130 — 165 CE), Alexandrian-born Christian teacher and founder of the Valentinian school, the most philosophically sophisticated Gnostic system of the 2nd century. Settled in Rome c. 136 — 165 CE; per Irenaeus (AH III.4.3) and Tertullian (Adv. Val. 4), he was a serious candidate for the bishopric of Rome before breaking with the proto-orthodox community. His direct writings survive only in fragments (Clement of Alexandria, Strom., preserves several; new evidence partially in Nag Hammadi: Gospel of Truth, possibly the Tripartite Tractate). The Valentinian system structures humanity into three classes — pneumatikoi (spiritual, predestined to gnosis), psychikoi (psychic, capable of choice and partial salvation), hylikoi (material, predestined to destruction) — a tripartition that Irenaeus (AH I, IV) and Tertullian read as destroying moral responsibility. Scholars (Linjamaa 2019, The Ethics of the Tripartite Tractate; Dunderberg) have argued that Valentinian determinism is more nuanced than the Patristic polemic suggests, but the polemic itself is the historical reality that shaped the development of free-will theology in Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Clement.

label: Marcion of Sinope
description: Marcion of Sinope (c. 85 — c. 160 CE), Pontic shipowner turned theologian, the most consequential 2nd-century opponent of the proto-orthodox Christian movement. Excommunicated at Rome c. 144 CE. Marcion postulated a radical dualism of two Gods: the just but inferior Demiurge of the Hebrew scriptures (the lawgiver and creator), and the supreme, hitherto unknown Good God revealed in Christ. He compiled the first Christian biblical canon — a redacted Gospel of Luke and ten Pauline epistles (the so-called Apostolikon), purged of what he regarded as Judaizing accretions. His writings survive only in citation by opponents, especially Tertullian's Adversus Marcionem (five books, c. 207 — 212 CE; CCSL 1; SC 365, 368, 399, 456, 483; ed. Braun) and Adamantius's Dialogue. For the free-will debate: Marcion's dualism removes moral evil from any free human origin by attributing the moral disorder of the world to the deficient Demiurge; Tertullian's Adv. Marc. II.5–9 grounds the orthodox response, defending liberum arbitrium as the metaphysical condition for genuine moral responsibility and as the locus of evil (not the Creator). Scholarship: Harnack 1924 (Marcion: das Evangelium vom fremden Gott); Moll 2010; Lieu 2015 (Marcion and the Making of a Heretic, CUP).

label: Monothelitism (μονοθελητισμός)
description: The Christological doctrine, advanced by Sergius I of Constantinople (610–638) and Patriarchs Pyrrhus, Paul II, and Macarius of Antioch with imperial support from Heraclius (Ekthesis, 638) and Constans II (Typos, 648), that Christ had only one will (θέλημα) — the divine will — and one operation (ἐνέργεια). The doctrine was a compromise intended to reconcile the Chalcedonian and Miaphysite parties of the empire. Theologically opposed by Sophronius of Jerusalem, Pope Martin I (Lateran Council 649), and most decisively by Maximus the Confessor, who, drawing on the Cappadocian distinction between will-as-natural-property and will-as-personal-mode, argued that to deny Christ a human natural will is to deny the integrity of Christ's human nature (which Chalcedon affirms). Maximus's Disputatio cum Pyrrho (645) and Opuscula develop the distinction between φυσικὸν θέλημα (natural will, proper to nature, hence two wills in Christ corresponding to two natures) and γνωμικὸν θέλημα (gnomic will, a deliberative mode of fallen rational agency, denied of Christ). Monothelitism was definitively condemned at the Sixth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople III, 680–681), which adopted Maximus's dyothelite Christology as Catholic doctrine. Maximus himself, condemned at the imperial council of 662, had his tongue and right hand cut off and died in exile in Lazica.
